name: The Binary Heap
statement: Keep the largest or smallest element at the root of a complete tree packed into an array.
statementAccent: the largest or smallest element at the root
meaning: A binary heap is a binary-tree-based data structure that satisfies the heap property and takes the form of a complete binary tree, meaning all levels are fully filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right. It is one of the most common ways to implement a priority queue. The heap property comes in two forms. In a max-heap, every parent node is greater than or equal to its children, so the maximum element sits at the root; in a min-heap, every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the minimum sits at the root. Because a binary heap is a complete binary tree, it can be stored compactly in an array without any pointers: for a node at index i in a zero-based array, its children are at indices two i plus one and two i plus two, and its parent is at the floor of i minus one over two. The main operations are efficient. Inserting an element and extracting the root, the minimum or maximum, both take order log n time, carried out by sifting an element up or down the tree to restore the heap property, while peeking at the root takes constant time, and building a heap from n elements takes order n time. Binary heaps give rise to heapsort, an order n log n comparison sort, and were introduced by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 as part of heapsort. They are used for priority queues, scheduling, selection, and as the priority queue inside graph algorithms such as Dijkstra's and Prim's.
mechanism: A binary heap maintains fast access to the extreme element, minimum or maximum, of a changing collection by keeping a weak ordering, the heap property, over a complete binary tree that is stored implicitly in an array. The heap property requires only that each parent compare correctly against its children, greater or equal in a max-heap, less or equal in a min-heap; it says nothing about the order between siblings, which is why a heap is much cheaper to maintain than a fully sorted structure while still keeping the extreme element at the root. Because the tree is complete, filled level by level and left to right, it maps perfectly onto an array with no wasted space and no pointers: a node at position i has children at two i plus one and two i plus two and a parent at the floor of i minus one over two, so navigation is pure arithmetic. To insert, one appends the new element at the end of the array, the next open leaf, then sifts it up, repeatedly swapping it with its parent while it violates the heap property, until it settles, which takes order log n steps because the tree's height is logarithmic. To extract the root, one moves the last element to the root position and sifts it down, repeatedly swapping it with its larger child in a max-heap, or smaller child in a min-heap, until the property is restored, again order log n. Peeking at the root is constant time, since the extreme element is always there. Building a heap from an arbitrary array can be done in order n time by sifting down from the last internal node upward, faster than inserting elements one by one. Heapsort exploits all this: it builds a heap and then repeatedly extracts the root, producing a sorted sequence in order n log n time.

examples.text: In a max-heap every parent is at least its children, so the maximum is always at the root.
A node at index i has children at two i plus one and two i plus two, so no pointers are needed.
Insertion sifts a new element up and extraction sifts the last element down, each in order log n.

variants.name: Min-heap and max-heap
variants.text: A min-heap keeps the smallest element at the root, a max-heap the largest, depending on the comparison used.

variants.name: Heapsort
variants.text: Building a heap and repeatedly extracting the root sorts n elements in order n log n time.

whyItMatters: The binary heap is one of the most useful and elegant data structures in computer science, the standard efficient way to implement a priority queue, a collection from which one repeatedly needs the most important, largest, or smallest element. Priority queues are everywhere: operating systems use them to schedule tasks by priority, event-driven simulations process events in time order, and many algorithms need to repeatedly pull the current best candidate. Above all, the binary heap is the priority queue that makes classic graph algorithms efficient: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm and Prim's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm both rely on repeatedly extracting the nearest or cheapest vertex, and a heap gives them their good running times. The heap also yields heapsort, an in-place comparison sort with a guaranteed order n log n worst case. Its beauty lies in doing all this with almost no overhead: because a complete binary tree packs perfectly into a plain array with children and parents found by simple index arithmetic, a binary heap needs no pointers and little memory, yet supports insertion and extraction in logarithmic time and constant-time access to the extreme element. Introduced by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 alongside heapsort, it remains a textbook structure and a practical workhorse. As the structure that keeps the largest or smallest element at the root of an array-packed complete tree, the binary heap is fundamental to priority scheduling and to graph and sorting algorithms.

working.text: store a complete binary tree in an array, with parent and child positions given by index arithmetic.
ensure each parent compares correctly against its children so the extreme element stays at the root.
sift a new element up on insertion and the last element down on extraction, each in order log n.

limits: The binary heap is efficient for its purpose but that purpose is specific, and several points reward care. It gives fast access only to the single extreme element, the minimum or maximum at the root; it does not keep the whole collection sorted, so it cannot efficiently find, say, the median or a general ranked element, nor search for an arbitrary key, which would take order n. It supports insertion, extraction of the root, and peeking, but operations like deleting or changing the priority of an arbitrary element require knowing that element's position and still cost order log n, and searching for it is slow. A binary heap is not a stable structure and imposes no order among siblings, so heapsort, though order n log n, is not stable. For some workloads other heap variants, such as binary heaps versus Fibonacci or pairing heaps, offer different trade-offs in the cost of operations like decrease-key, relevant to algorithms like Dijkstra's. Some details reward care: the array indexing two i plus one and two i plus two is for zero-based arrays, binary heaps were introduced by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 with heapsort, and building a heap is order n while heapsort overall is order n log n. So the binary heap robustly implements a priority queue, understood as a structure optimized for the extreme element rather than for general search or full ordering.
misreadings: The binary heap is not a sorted structure; it keeps only the extreme element at the root, not the whole collection in order. It does not support fast search for arbitrary elements, which costs order n. And heapsort, though order n log n, is not stable, so treating a heap as fully sorted, as searchable like a search tree, or as giving a stable sort, misreads it.
origin: The array-based complete-binary-tree priority-queue structure introduced by J. W. J. Williams in 1964 with heapsort, keeping the largest or smallest element at the root via the heap property.
